draft.title: The sine rule
card: In any triangle, a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Each side is opposite the angle with the same letter.

Use it when you know an angle and the side opposite it, plus one more side or angle. Write two of the ratios, then solve for the unknown. Example: A = 30°, a = 5, B = 90° gives b = 5 × sin 90° ÷ sin 30° = 10.
To find an angle, flip the rule: sin B = b sin A ÷ a. A calculator gives only an acute angle for B, but an obtuse angle 180° − B has the same sine.

Ambiguous case: when you know two sides and an angle opposite one of them, two triangles can fit. The second angle 180° − B works if it still leaves room for the given angle, so the two angles add to less than 180°.
draft.remember: Match each side with its opposite angle. A sine can come from an acute angle or its obtuse partner.

a.q: In triangle PQR, angle P = 40°, angle Q = 70° and QR = 10 cm. What is the length of PR, to 1 decimal place?
a.why: QR is opposite P and PR is opposite Q. So PR = 10 × sin 70° ÷ sin 40° = 14.6 cm. Putting the sines the wrong way round gives 6.8 cm.
a.clue: Pair each side with the angle opposite it.

b.q: In triangle ABC, angle A = 30°, a = 8 cm and b = 12 cm. Using the sine rule, a calculator gives B = 48.6°. What is the other possible size of angle B?
b.why: Two triangles fit, because sin B = 12 × sin 30° ÷ 8 = 0.75 has an acute and an obtuse answer. The other angle is 180° − 48.6° = 131.4°, and 30° + 131.4° is less than 180°, so it works. 101.4° is the third angle of the first triangle, not another B.
b.clue: An obtuse angle shares its sine with an acute one.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers check out: PR = 10 sin 70° ÷ sin 40° ≈ 14.6 cm, and the obtuse case B = 131.4° is valid because 30° + 131.4° < 180°.
